\section[vadāmi]{\sk{वदामि} (vadāmi) — \textquotedblleft{}I speak,\textquotedblright{} and the Sanskrit verb}

\label{lesson:SA-C05-vadami}



\begin{quote}
So far, \textquotedblleft{}to be.\textquotedblright{} Here is a verb that \emph{acts} — and it reveals the most famous feature of the Sanskrit verb: it counts to \textbf{three}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{va · dā · mi}. The long \emph{ā} in the middle beat is the ending doing its work — shorten it and the word stops meaning \textquotedblleft{}I speak.\textquotedblright{}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vadāmi} (\textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{}) is from the root \emph{vad} (\textquotedblleft{}to speak, to say\textquotedblright{}) — the very root of \emph{vāda} (\textquotedblleft{}a saying\textquotedblright{}) inside Chapter 1's \emph{dhanyavādaḥ} (\textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{}). The present tense is stem + person- ending: \emph{vad-ā-mi}, where \emph{-mi} means \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} — the same \emph{-mi} you can see in \emph{asmi} (\textquotedblleft{}I am\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: singular, DUAL, and plural}]
Here is Sanskrit's showpiece. Where English (and Hindi) count in two — singular and plural — Sanskrit counts in \textbf{three}, with a special \textbf{dual} for \emph{exactly two}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{form} & \textbf{meaning} \\
\midrule
singular & \emph{vadāmi} & I speak \\
\textbf{dual} & \emph{vadāvaḥ} & \textbf{we two} speak \\
plural & \emph{vadāmaḥ} & we (three or more) speak \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A whole grammatical number just for pairs — for two eyes, two hands, a couple. Greek had it too, and lost it; English never kept it; Sanskrit polished it. It is one of the things that makes the language feel so exact.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vadāmi\textquotedblright{} — I speak
  \item the root and its Chapter-1 cousin (\emph{vad}; \emph{dhanyavāda}, \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{})
  \item the three numbers — \emph{vadāmi} (I) / \emph{vadāvaḥ} (we two) / \emph{vadāmaḥ} (we all)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root is \emph{vadāmi} from, and what third \textquotedblleft{}number\textquotedblright{} does Sanskrit have that English lacks? (\emph{Vad}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}; the \textbf{dual}, for exactly two — \emph{vadāvaḥ}, \textquotedblleft{}we two speak.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ya]{\sk{य} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S204-letter-ya}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{◌ु} · \sk{र} · \sk{प}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{य}}
\textbf{\sk{य}} — \emph{ya}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{y}, it is \textbf{ya}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a clockwise inner curl
  \item a lower bowl rising to the right-stem junction
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these words, and \sk{य} is one of the shapes inside them — the rest of their shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dhanyavādaḥ} — thank you
  \item \emph{punardarśanāya} — until we meet again (lit. \textquotedblleft{}for seeing again\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{य}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start beneath the headline, curve clockwise around the inner curl, and finish at the left waist
  \item \textbf{2.} lift at that waist, curve down and right around the lower bowl, and rise to the right-stem junction
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified four-stroke teaching form; another animated learner source joins the inner curl and lower bowl
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\sk{य}-order.gif’, strokes 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{य} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{य}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{य} three times, saying \emph{ya} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{य} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{य}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ya}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ahaṁ saṁskṛtaṁ vadāmi]{\sk{अहं} \sk{संस्कृतं} \sk{वदामि} (ahaṁ saṁskṛtaṁ vadāmi) — \textquotedblleft{}I speak Sanskrit\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:SA-C05-aham-samskritam-vadami}



\begin{quote}
Your first full, moving sentence — and the language's name is itself a little lesson in how Sanskrit builds words.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{a · haṁ · saṁs · kṛ · taṁ · va · dā · mi}. The \emph{ṁ} is a hum through the nose that colours the vowel before it rather than a full \emph{m}; \emph{ṛ} is a short vowel made with the tongue curled, near the \emph{ri} of \emph{rich}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ahaṁ saṁskṛtaṁ vadāmi} = \emph{aham} (\textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{saṁskṛtam} (the object) + \emph{vadāmi} (\textquotedblleft{}speak\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}I Sanskrit speak,\textquotedblright{} the verb last (as in every daughter language). The name \emph{saṁskṛta} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{put together, refined, perfected}\textquotedblright{} — from \emph{sam-} (\textquotedblleft{}together,\textquotedblright{} cousin of English \emph{same}, Greek \emph{syn-}) + \emph{kṛta} (\textquotedblleft{}made, done,\textquotedblright{} from the root \emph{kṛ} you met in \emph{namaskāra}). So \textquotedblleft{}Sanskrit\textquotedblright{} literally means \textquotedblleft{}the perfected {[}language{]},\textquotedblright{} named in contrast to \emph{prākṛta} (\textquotedblleft{}natural, raw\textquotedblright{} — Prakrit, the everyday speech from which Hindi, Bengali, and the rest descend).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: sandhi joins the words}]
Say it aloud and \emph{aham} + \emph{saṁskṛtam} runs together as \emph{ahaṁ saṁskṛtam} — the \emph{m} softening to the anusvāra before the next consonant. That is \textbf{sandhi}, the sound-joining you met in Chapter 1's \emph{svāgatam}; it is why Sanskrit flows.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ahaṁ saṁskṛtaṁ vadāmi\textquotedblright{}
  \item what \emph{saṁskṛta} means (\emph{sam} \textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{} + \emph{kṛta} \textquotedblleft{}made\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}perfected\textquotedblright{})
  \item its opposite, the source of the modern languages (\emph{prākṛta}, \textquotedblleft{}natural\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I speak Sanskrit,\textquotedblright{} and unpack the name. (\emph{Ahaṁ saṁskṛtaṁ vadāmi}; \emph{saṁskṛta} = \emph{sam} \textquotedblleft{}together\textquotedblright{} + \emph{kṛta} \textquotedblleft{}made\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}the perfected language.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vasāmi]{\sk{वसामि} (vasāmi) — \textquotedblleft{}I live, I dwell\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:SA-C05-vasami}



\begin{quote}
A second verb, so you can say where you live — and it hides the English word \emph{was}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{va · sā · mi}. One consonant apart from \emph{vadāmi}, and the same long \emph{ā} carrying the ending.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vasāmi} (\textquotedblleft{}I dwell, I live\textquotedblright{}) is from the root \emph{vas} (\textquotedblleft{}to dwell, to stay, to abide\textquotedblright{}), from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*wes-} (\textquotedblleft{}to dwell, to be\textquotedblright{}) — the ancestor of English \textbf{was} and \textbf{were} (the past of \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} began as \textquotedblleft{}to dwell/remain\textquotedblright{}). So Sanskrit's \textquotedblleft{}I dwell\textquotedblright{} and English's \textquotedblleft{}was\textquotedblright{} are, at the root, one word. From \emph{vas} come \emph{vāsa} (\textquotedblleft{}a dwelling\textquotedblright{}), \emph{nivāsa} (\textquotedblleft{}a residence\textquotedblright{}), and names like \emph{Vārāṇasī}. \textquotedblleft{}I live in the city\textquotedblright{} is \emph{ahaṁ nagare vasāmi}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} is a case-ending}]
\emph{nagare} (\textquotedblleft{}in the city\textquotedblright{}) = \emph{nagara} (\textquotedblleft{}city\textquotedblright{}) in the \textbf{locative} case (\emph{-e}, \textquotedblleft{}in / at\textquotedblright{}). Sanskrit has no separate word for \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} — it is folded into the noun's ending, the ancestor of the postpositions Hindi and Bengali use. This is your second case, after Chapter 4's dative.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vasāmi\textquotedblright{} — I dwell
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I live in the city\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ahaṁ nagare vasāmi}
  \item the English cousin of the root \emph{vas} (\textbf{was})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What PIE root is \emph{vasāmi} from, its English cousin, and how does Sanskrit say \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{*wes-} \textquotedblleft{}to dwell\textquotedblright{}; English \textbf{was}; with a case-ending, the locative \emph{-e}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṛ]{\sk{◌ृ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S205-vowel-sign-vocalic-r}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{र} · \sk{प} · \sk{य}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{◌ृ}}
\textbf{\sk{◌ृ}} — \emph{ṛ}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

Where it sits: a small hook below (the vocalic r, common in Sanskrit).

Worked through: \textbf{\sk{न}} + \textbf{\sk{◌ृ}} = \textbf{\sk{नृ}} — \emph{nṛ}.

You already say this word, and \sk{◌ृ} is one of the shapes inside it — the rest of its shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ahaṁ saṁskṛtaṁ vadāmi} — I speak Sanskrit
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{◌ृ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \sk{◌ृ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{◌ृ} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{◌ृ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{◌ृ} three times, saying \emph{ṛ} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{◌ृ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{◌ृ}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{ṛ} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[karomi]{\sk{करोमि} (karomi) — \textquotedblleft{}I do,\textquotedblright{} from the root behind \emph{karma} and \emph{namaskāra}}

\label{lesson:SA-C05-karomi}



\begin{quote}
The last verb of the chapter — from the single most productive root in Sanskrit, one you have met again and again.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\emph{ka · ro · mi}. Three even beats, all short.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{karomi} (\textquotedblleft{}I do, I make\textquotedblright{}) is from the root \emph{kṛ} (\textquotedblleft{}to do, make\textquotedblright{}), from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}er-}. This is the root at the heart of this book:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{namaskāraḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{making} of a bow\textquotedblright{} (\emph{namas} + \emph{kāra})
  \item \emph{karma} — \textquotedblleft{}a thing \textbf{done},\textquotedblright{} an action
  \item \emph{saṁskṛta} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{put together}, perfected\textquotedblright{} (this very language)
\end{itemize}

To say \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I work},\textquotedblright{} Sanskrit says \emph{kāryaṁ karomi} — \textquotedblleft{}I do work,\textquotedblright{} where \emph{kāryam} (\textquotedblleft{}work, task\textquotedblright{}) is \emph{itself} from \emph{kṛ} (\textquotedblleft{}a thing-to-be-done\textquotedblright{}). So \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} is, at root, \textquotedblleft{}\emph{kṛ}-thing I \emph{kṛ}-do.\textquotedblright{} Hindi's \emph{kām karnā} and Bengali's \emph{kāj karā} are its worn-down grandchildren.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}karomi\textquotedblright{} — I do
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} — \emph{kāryaṁ karomi}
  \item three words from the root \emph{kṛ} (\emph{namaskāra}, \emph{karma}, \emph{saṁskṛta})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root is \emph{karomi} from, and name three words built on it. (\emph{Kṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}to do,\textquotedblright{} PIE \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}er-}; \emph{namaskāra}, \emph{karma}, \emph{saṁskṛta} — among many.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 5 — The first verbs}

\label{lesson:SA-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three verbs, one engine — and Sanskrit's count-to-three.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I speak Sanskrit\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ahaṁ saṁskṛtaṁ vadāmi}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I live in the city\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ahaṁ nagare vasāmi}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ahaṁ kāryaṁ karomi}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}we two speak\textquotedblright{} — \emph{vadāvaḥ} (the dual!)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{How to answer: the engine}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the ending that means \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} (\emph{-mi}, as in \emph{asmi}, \emph{vadāmi})
  \item Sanskrit's three numbers (singular / \textbf{dual} / plural)
  \item where the verb sits, and how \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} is shown (verb last; a case-ending, the locative \emph{-e})
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: the roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vad} \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{} ($\to$ \emph{dhanyavāda})
  \item \emph{vas} \textquotedblleft{}to dwell\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*wes-} $\to$ English \textbf{was}
  \item \emph{kṛ} \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}er-} $\to$ the root of \emph{namaskāra}, \emph{karma}, \emph{saṁskṛta}; \emph{kāryam} \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{saṁskṛta} = \emph{sam} (\textquotedblleft{}together,\textquotedblright{} English \emph{same}) + \emph{kṛta} (\textquotedblleft{}made\textquotedblright{}) = \textquotedblleft{}perfected\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In one breath, say your language, your city, and your work in Sanskrit — then say \textquotedblleft{}we two speak.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Ahaṁ saṁskṛtaṁ vadāmi. Ahaṁ nagare vasāmi. Ahaṁ kāryaṁ karomi. Vadāvaḥ.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a]{\sk{अ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S03-letter-a}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{प} · \sk{य} · \sk{◌ृ}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{अ}}
\textbf{\sk{अ}} — \emph{a}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel}: the full-size letter a vowel wears when it opens a word and has no consonant to lean on. Inside a word the same vowel is written as a small sign instead.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a joined upper-and-lower left body
  \item a middle shoulder
  \item a right vertical stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these words, and \sk{अ} is one of the shapes inside them — the rest of their shapes are still ahead of you, so here the character stands on its own:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{asti} — is
  \item \emph{mama nāma … asti} — my name is…
  \item \emph{bhavān katham asti?} — how are you?
  \item \emph{aham} — I
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{अ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} curve around the upper bowl, then continue down and around the lower bowl without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and sweep the middle shoulder right
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{4.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 3.} The pen comes up 3 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified modern printed teaching form; other Devanagari traditions split the body into more strokes
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \sk{अ} stroke order.svg’, frames 1–4, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{अ} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{अ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{अ} three times, saying \emph{a} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{अ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{अ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{a}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
